lead: This unit explains what a mobile operating system does, how the Android platform and its SDK are put together, and how an app is built from activities, intents and fragments. After it you can read an Android project, trace an activity through its life cycle, and wire two screens together with an intent or a fragment.
about: The unit moves from the general to the specific. Chapter 2.1 compares the main mobile operating systems and what each one owns. Chapter 2.2 opens the Android stack and the SDK tools that sit on top of it. Chapter 2.3 takes a first project apart file by file. Chapter 2.4 makes the activity and its life cycle the centre of the app. Chapter 2.5 uses intents to move between activities and to hand work to apps already on the phone. Chapter 2.6 breaks a screen into fragments and shows the specialised fragment types. Each chapter assumes the one before it, so the life cycle in 2.4 is read against the components named in 2.3, and the intents in 2.5 are read against the activities of 2.4.

chapters.idea: A mobile operating system is the layer that manages the phone's hardware, sandboxes apps and controls how apps are installed and paid for.
chapters.depth: What an OS does on a phone: process and memory management, power management, sandboxing, permissions, app store and payment. Compare Android (Linux kernel, ART runtime, Java and Kotlin, open source core with Google Play services), iOS (Darwin kernel, Swift and Objective-C, closed, App Store, builds need a Mac) and Windows Phone (C# and XAML, Metro/Modern UI, now legacy). Some syllabi call this 'commercial mobile operating systems' and add BlackBerry, also legacy. Keep one line each on m-commerce and app-store billing; the network generations GSM, GPRS and UMTS belong to Unit 1.

figure.aria: A tree with one root labelled Mobile OS and four children, each naming an operating system and its kernel or store model.

chapters.example: A team must ship the same to-do app on Android, iOS and Windows Phone. For each platform state the main language, the build tool, the store and the one extra requirement. Answer: Android uses Java or Kotlin, built in Android Studio with Gradle, sold through Google Play, and needs no special machine. iOS uses Swift or Objective-C, built in Xcode, sold through the App Store, and needs a Mac. Windows Phone used C# and XAML in Visual Studio and its own Store, and is no longer developed, so the to-do app ships on two platforms only.
chapters.trap: Writing that Android is a Linux distribution in the Ubuntu sense. Only the kernel is Linux; the framework, runtime and store above it are Google's. The second trap is quoting a platform version such as Android 13 without its API level.
chapters.prereq: Unit 1 for what a cellular network does; nothing else.
chapters.leave: GSM, GPRS and UMTS details to Unit 1; iOS tooling, UIKit and segues to Unit 6; app-store publishing and m-commerce checkout flow to Unit 5.

chapters.idea: The Android platform is a fixed stack of layers, and the SDK is the set of tools that compiles and installs code against one chosen layer of that stack.
chapters.depth: Draw the stack from the bottom: Linux kernel (drivers, power, process isolation), HAL, native libraries (SQLite, OpenGL ES, WebKit) plus the Android runtime ART running DEX bytecode, the Java API framework (Activity, View, ContentProvider, NotificationManager), and system apps. Then the SDK: Android Studio, SDK Manager with platforms and build-tools, platform-tools with adb, the emulator and AVDs, Gradle, Logcat, lint, d8 and AAPT2. Define API level as the integer that names a platform version, and show compileSdk, minSdk and targetSdk in build.gradle. Framework classes are named here but used in Unit 3.

figure.aria: A six-layer stack from system apps down to the Linux kernel, with the Java API framework picked out and a side note running from app code to hardware.

chapters.example: A module's build.gradle sets compileSdk 34, minSdk 24 and targetSdk 34. A tester's phone reports API 21. Explain the three numbers and say what the tester sees. Answer: compileSdk 34 means the code is compiled against the Android 14 framework, so API 34 calls type-check. minSdk 24 means the APK refuses to install on anything below API 24, so the API 21 phone fails with INSTALL_FAILED_OLDER_SDK and the store hides the app from it. targetSdk 34 means the app opts in to Android 14 behaviour changes, such as stricter background rules. Raising minSdk to 21 would let that phone install, but every API 24 call would need a runtime check.
chapters.trap: Swapping compileSdk and targetSdk, or treating Android Studio as the SDK. The SDK is the platform, build-tools and platform-tools; Studio is only the editor in front of it.
chapters.prereq: Chapter 2.1 for what an OS layer is.
chapters.leave: Layouts, views and event handling to Unit 3; file and database APIs to Unit 4; signing and releasing APKs to Unit 5.

chapters.idea: An Android project is a small fixed set of files, and R is the generated class that lets Java code point at XML resources.
chapters.depth: Only a few universities teach this at this depth, so keep it short. Trace a generated project: build.gradle for the module, AndroidManifest.xml naming the launcher activity, MainActivity.java with onCreate and setContentView, res/layout/activity_main.xml holding the view tree, res/values/strings.xml holding text, and the generated R class. Say how AAPT2 turns each XML file and each string into an int constant in R, so R.layout.activity_main and R.id.button1 are ints, not files. Show one run on an emulator and where Logcat prints.

figure.aria: A project folder tree with the app folder holding manifests, java sources, resources and the module build file.

chapters.example: A new project called HelloApp uses package com.example.hello with one empty activity. Name the files you edit to show the words 'Hello, Chennai' and say what each edit does. Answer: res/values/strings.xml gets <string name="greeting">Hello, Chennai</string>. res/layout/activity_main.xml gets a TextView with android:text="@string/greeting". The build turns that into R.string.greeting and R.id for the view. MainActivity.java keeps setContentView(R.layout.activity_main) so the layout is inflated, and adds findViewById(R.id.text1) only if the text must change at run time. AndroidManifest.xml needs the activity with the MAIN action and LAUNCHER category, or nothing opens.
chapters.trap: Editing XML and expecting the running app to change without a rebuild, or writing the R import by hand. A red R almost always means a resource error, not a missing import.
chapters.prereq: Chapter 2.2 for the SDK and API level.
chapters.leave: Anything about how views are measured, styled or laid out to Unit 3; storage of user data to Unit 4.

chapters.idea: An activity is one screen with a life cycle, and Android calls a fixed order of methods as the screen becomes visible, gets covered and is destroyed.
chapters.depth: Declare the activity in the manifest with an intent filter. Cover the seven callbacks onCreate, onStart, onResume, onPause, onStop, onDestroy, onRestart and the four states (created, started, resumed, destroyed) they define. Make clear the difference between visible and foreground. Treat rotation as destroy-and-recreate and use onSaveInstanceState with a Bundle to carry small state. Show the back stack and a task in one line. Use Logcat to read the order.

figure.aria: A flow of activity callbacks from onCreate down to onDestroy, with a dashed return path from onStop back to onStart through onRestart.

chapters.example: Log the callbacks of one activity, then perform four actions and write the order. Actions: (a) launch the app, (b) press Home, (c) reopen it from the recent list, (d) press Back. Answer: (a) onCreate, onStart, onResume. (b) onPause, onStop, because the activity is fully hidden. (c) onRestart, onStart, onResume. (d) onPause, onStop, onDestroy, because Back removes the activity from the back stack. Now rotate the phone while the activity is resumed: onPause, onStop, onDestroy, then onCreate, onStart, onResume for a fresh instance, which is why a count of 7 in a plain int field comes back as 0 and needs onSaveInstanceState.
chapters.trap: Saying onPause means the activity is destroyed. It is still alive and may still be visible. Second trap: assuming onDestroy always runs before the process is killed, which it does not.
chapters.prereq: Chapter 2.3 for the activity class, manifest entry and setContentView.
chapters.leave: View layout and widget behaviour to Unit 3; saving that state to disk or a database to Unit 4.

chapters.idea: An intent is a message object: an explicit intent names the activity to open, and an implicit intent names an action the system matches to any app that can handle it.
chapters.depth: Only a few universities teach this in detail, so stay brief. Explicit intent with component name versus implicit intent with action, category, data Uri and extras. Intent filters in the manifest, and the resolveActivity or PackageManager check before startActivity. Built-ins to name: ACTION_DIAL, ACTION_CALL, ACTION_VIEW, ACTION_SEND, ACTION_SENDTO, ACTION_PICK. Mention extras keys and the deprecation of startActivityForResult in favour of the Activity Result API, in one sentence.

figure.aria: A message sequence where the app calls startActivity, the Android system matches an intent filter and launches the target app.

chapters.example: A restaurant screen has two buttons. 'Call' should open the dialer with 9876543210 filled in, and 'Share' should send the text 'Table for 4' to whichever app the user picks. Write both intents. Answer: call is new Intent(Intent.ACTION_DIAL, Uri.parse("tel:9876543210")); startActivity(call). ACTION_DIAL fills the dialer and needs no permission; ACTION_CALL would place the call directly and needs CALL_PHONE. Share is new Intent(Intent.ACTION_SEND); share.setType("text/plain"); share.putExtra(Intent.EXTRA_TEXT, "Table for 4"); startActivity(Intent.createChooser(share, "Send via")). createChooser shows the app list; without it the system picks a default and may throw ActivityNotFoundException if nothing matches.
chapters.trap: Firing an implicit intent without checking that any app can handle it, then crashing with ActivityNotFoundException. Second trap: using ACTION_CALL where ACTION_DIAL is enough, and forgetting the permission.
chapters.prereq: Chapter 2.4 for what an activity is and how it is declared.
chapters.leave: Sending SMS and e-mail in code, maps and location to Unit 5; iOS segues, which do the same job differently, to Unit 6.

chapters.idea: A fragment is a reusable piece of screen with its own life cycle that lives inside an activity and is added, replaced or removed by the FragmentManager.
chapters.depth: Why fragments exist: one activity, several panes, reuse on tablets. Fragment life cycle callbacks (onAttach, onCreate, onCreateView, onViewCreated, onStart, onResume, onPause, onStop, onDestroyView, onDetach) tied to the host, never equal to it. FragmentManager and FragmentTransaction: add, replace, remove, addToBackStack, commit; the container view id. Data in an arguments Bundle, communication through the host activity or the Fragment Result API, not a direct fragment-to-fragment call. Configuration change and the sw600dp two-pane layout. Specialised types: ListFragment, DialogFragment, PreferenceFragmentCompat.

figure.aria: A host activity using FragmentManager to add a list fragment into a container, with a dashed edge to a detail fragment when the user taps an item.

chapters.example: A master-detail app shows a list of 3 items in a ListFragment. On a 360 dp wide phone, tapping item 2 must open the detail on a second screen; on a 900 dp tablet the list and detail sit side by side. Describe both paths. Answer: the layout folder res/layout holds an activity with one FrameLayout container (id list_container). res/layout-sw600dp holds an activity with two containers, ids list_container and detail_container. At start the activity adds the ListFragment to list_container and, only if detail_container exists (findViewById returns non-null), adds a DetailFragment with arguments item = 1. On the phone, tapping item 2 starts the detail through the host activity; the host calls replace(R.id.list_container, detailFragment) and addToBackStack(null), so Back returns to the list. On the tablet the host sends item = 2 to the fragment already in detail_container with setArguments and a replace, keeping the list visible.
chapters.trap: Calling getActivity() after the fragment is detached and getting null, or calling commit() after onSaveInstanceState and crashing. Also, treating the fragment life cycle as identical to the activity life cycle.
chapters.prereq: Chapter 2.4 for the activity life cycle; Chapter 2.3 for layouts and the R class.
chapters.leave: View types and styling to Unit 3; shared data through ViewModel or database to Unit 4; the iOS split view controller equivalent to Unit 6.
